item.title: Government warns tourism industry against further delays to 5% tourism services tax
item.description: Finance Minister Esrom Immanuel says Government has given the tourism industry sufficient time to prepare for the introduction of the 5 percent Tourism Services Tax (TST), warning that further attempts to delay its implementation will not be accepted. The Government has accused the Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association (FHTA) and some tourism operators of using “delaying tactics” and negative publici
item.content:encoded:
Finance Minister Esrom Immanuel says Government has given the tourism industry sufficient time to prepare for the introduction of the 5 percent Tourism Services Tax (TST), warning that further attempts to delay its implementation will not be accepted.

The Government has accused the Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association (FHTA) and some tourism operators of using “delaying tactics” and negative publicity to undermine the new tax.

Finance Minister Esrom Immanuel said the Government had engaged with the FHTA and key tourism stakeholders since June and had already extended the implementation date three times — from July 1 to August 1 and then to September 1.

“These extensions were provided in good faith to allow the industry sufficient time to prepare its systems, communicate with customers and ensure compliance,” Mr Immanuel said.

He said Government was concerned that some industry players, with the support of the FHTA, continued to create negative publicity around the tax.

“Government believes that these actions risk undermining and sabotaging a measure that is in the broader interest of Fiji’s tourism industry and the national economy,” he said.

Mr Immanuel said the 5 percent TST was introduced as part of broader Government efforts to support Fiji Airways, which he described as critical to the survival and growth of the tourism industry.

“Protecting Fiji Airways means protecting the connectivity on which hotels, resorts, tour operators, restaurants, transport operators, cruise services and thousands of other tourism-related businesses depend,” he said.

The Minister said tourism contributes about 40 percent of economic activity, generates nearly $3 billion in foreign exchange earnings and supports thousands of jobs and businesses.

He also defended the tax by pointing to the significant incentives the tourism industry had received over many years, including tax holidays, duty concessions and taxpayer-funded tourism marketing.

“Today, the entire tourism industry contributes only around 5 percent of the total corporate taxes collected by Government. The other 95 percent is paid by non-tourism sectors,” Mr Immanuel said.

He said the industry had a responsibility to contribute to the wider national effort when critical tourism infrastructure, including the national airline, required support.

Mr Immanuel also compared the new tax with tourism-related taxes imposed under the previous Government.

He said the tourism sector was previously subject to a combined 16 percent turnover-based tax through the 10 percent ECAL and 6 percent STT.

“The current Tourism Services Tax is 5 percent, is turnover-based and is being introduced as a temporary measure for only 12 months,” he said.

According to the Minister, the Government had deliberately designed the measure to focus on larger tourism operators so that smaller businesses would not be unnecessarily burdened.

He said Government remained willing to address practical concerns and clarify issues surrounding implementation.

“However, the tourism industry must now work constructively with Government to implement the TST rather than continue attempts to delay or undermine it,” Mr Immanuel said.

The Tourism Services Tax is scheduled to take effect on September 1, 2026.

item.title: Teachers call for stronger Human Resource section
item.description: THE Fiji Head Teachers Association (FHTA) is calling for a strengthened human resources section within the Ministry of Education to provide more effective and timely support to teachers and heads of schools. Speaking at the 43rd FHTA annual conference, FHTA president Johnson Rura said the ministry needed a human resources section staffed by officers with in-depth knowledge of schools across Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Head Teachers Association (FHTA) is calling for a strengthened human resources section within the Ministry of Education to provide more effective and timely support to teachers and heads of schools.

Speaking at the 43rd FHTA annual conference, FHTA president Johnson Rura said the ministry needed a human resources section staffed by officers with in-depth knowledge of schools across Fiji.

“Such a department must be responsive, professional and proactive, ensuring that teachers and heads of schools receive the support they need without unnecessary delays,” he said.

Mr Rura also raised concerns about repatriation arrangements for deceased education officers.

He said the association had lost 14 members since its last conference and the number of teachers dying continued to increase each year.

“This is a painful reality for our association.

“As an employer, the ministry has rightly paid travelling allowances when we are posted to new schools.

“We respectfully submit that the same principle should apply if the Almighty calls one of our officers to rest while still serving under the Ministry of Education at their work station.

“We, therefore, call for clear and consistent implementation of ministry-funded repatriation arrangements for deceased education officers.”

Mr Rura said the process would ensure grieving families and colleagues were not placed under additional financial pressure during an already difficult time.

“We understand that a draft policy has already gone through its first consultation.”

Mr Rura appealed to the Minister for Education Aseri Radrodro to ensure the policy was implemented during his tenure.

item.title: Electoral laws to be pushed ahead
item.description: JUSTICE Minister and Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga has defended the Government’s decision to fast-track three electoral reform Bills, saying the urgency was driven by Fiji’s approaching election. Mr Turaga moved in Parliament for the Electoral Amendment Bill 2026, the Political Parties Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures Amendment Bill 2026 and the Electoral Registration of Vote
item.content:encoded:
JUSTICE Minister and Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga has defended the Government’s decision to fast-track three electoral reform Bills, saying the urgency was driven by Fiji’s approaching election.

Mr Turaga moved in Parliament for the Electoral Amendment Bill 2026, the Political Parties Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures Amendment Bill 2026 and the Electoral Registration of Voters Amendment Bill 2026 to be considered without delay.

He said the reforms were necessary to modernise Fiji’s electoral framework, strengthen transparency and address issues identified through consultations and observer reports.

“There’s a reason why it was brought under Standing Order 51, because of the urgency,” Mr Turaga said.

He said the proposed changes had broad political support and would make the electoral system more open while strengthening accountability.

“Most of the issues that Honourable Usamate referred to, they basically are common. The other party, this party, the three parties, they agree that there should be a change in which elections are conducted.”

Mr Turaga acknowledged concerns about the limited timeframe but said the committee had about a month to deliberate on the legislation.

“I’m sure you will come to an agreement.”

Responding to Mr Usamate’s concerns that Parliament needed more time for its own consultations, Mr Turaga said the Bills were interconnected and committee members had significant experience.

“The bills are related. And the members are from a lived experience.

“I believe that through the experience of this committee, they have been dedicated, committed to the work that they have done the last three years.”

All three motions were agreed to without opposition, with the Bills referred to the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights for consideration before the September sitting.

item.title: New measures to protect citizens
item.description: FIJI is stepping up efforts to build a digitally connected and cyber-secure nation, with the Government advancing new measures to protect citizens, strengthen online safety and improve access to public services. Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua told Parliament on Thursday that Government had moved from planning to implementation under its National Digital Strategy 2025–203
item.content:encoded:
FIJI is stepping up efforts to build a digitally connected and cyber-secure nation, with the Government advancing new measures to protect citizens, strengthen online safety and improve access to public services.

Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua told Parliament on Thursday that Government had moved from planning to implementation under its National Digital Strategy 2025–2030 and National Cybersecurity and Resilience Strategy 2026–2031.

He said Government had established a National Computer Emergency Response Team to assist organisations in recovering from cyber incidents and had strengthened its Government Data Centre and 24/7 Network and Security Operations Centre.

He said Fiji had also rolled out 5G technology and launched a national cybersecurity website to provide information and allow people to report cyber incidents and online harm.

“We delivered, our National Cyber Security Website —one trusted home for Fijians to turn to for guidance on reporting a cyber incident or online harm, and to cyber information,” Mr Naivalurua said.

He said Fiji also became the first Pacific nation and 50th globally, to sign the Second Additional Protocol to the Budapest Convention.

“Once ratified, it will give our law enforcement faster international cooperation to pursue cybercriminals across borders.”

He said work was continuing on an Online Safety Law review, telecommunications legislation and a national identification initiative.

The digitalFIJI e-Profile is expected to be tabled in Parliament next month, providing every Fijian with one secure identity for accessing Government, health, financial and social services.

Mr Naivalurua said data protection legislation was also progressing before amendments to Fiji’s Cybercrime law could proceed.

item.title: Overcrowded emergency unit to undergo expansion works
item.description: OVERCROWDING at the Emergency Department of Colonial War Memorial Hospital is being attributed primarily to a shortage of space, with Health Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu confirming that an expansion is planned. The issue was raised in Parliament after Opposition MP Rinesh Sharma described the Emergency Department at the Suva hospital as overcrowded and chaotic, with critical patients sometimes fo
item.content:encoded:
OVERCROWDING at the Emergency Department of Colonial War Memorial Hospital is being attributed primarily to a shortage of space, with Health Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu confirming that an expansion is planned.

The issue was raised in Parliament after Opposition MP Rinesh Sharma described the Emergency Department at the Suva hospital as overcrowded and chaotic, with critical patients sometimes forced to sit on benches while doctors and nurses work under pressure.

Mr Sharma asked whether temporary structures could be introduced while the department awaited expansion.

Dr Lalabalavu said the Emergency Department expansion formed part of the Pacific Healthy Islands Transformation Project, which included plans to expand the Accident and Emergency area.

The minister later confirmed that the problem at the Emergency Department was a “space issue” after Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu asked whether patients waiting for more than a day without beds reflected a shortage of beds, space or both.

Meanwhile, concerns were also raised about the care and misuse of hospital equipment.

MP Alvick Maharaj questioned who would be held responsible when wheelchairs, fixtures and other expensive equipment were damaged or abused.

Dr Lalabalavu said responsibility rested with everyone using or managing public assets, with nursing supervisors responsible for monitoring equipment within hospital wards and reporting damage or misuse.

The Government’s hospital upgrade program is expected to improve both patient care and the condition of medical facilities nationwide.

item.title: Usamate cautions reform haste
item.description: OPPOSITION Member of Parliament Jone Usamate has warned Parliament against rushing major electoral reforms, saying parliamentary committees need adequate time to scrutinise proposed changes in the Bill. Mr Usamate made the comments in Parliament during debate on the Electoral Amendment Bill 2026, which the Government wants fast-tracked ahead of the September sitting.
item.content:encoded:
OPPOSITION Member of Parliament Jone Usamate has warned Parliament against rushing major electoral reforms, saying parliamentary committees need adequate time to scrutinise proposed changes in the Bill.

Mr Usamate made the comments in Parliament during debate on the Electoral Amendment Bill 2026, which the Government wants fast-tracked ahead of the September sitting.

He said while the Political Parties Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures Amendment Bill 2026 contained a manageable number of amendments and could potentially be considered by September, the Electoral Amendment Bill presented a much bigger challenge.

“When you take this Bill and the other bill that you’ve just gone through, the one that was presented earlier, which is the Amendment to the Electoral Act, which has around 47 amendments,” Mr Usamate said.

“This other one, and I speak very frankly, because it needs to be looked at very carefully, it’ll be very difficult to deliver that one in one month.”

Mr Usamate said the committee’s role was different from the executive’s consultation process and should not be compressed into a single month.

“You must also give time to the people that represent the people, the legislature, to also carry out its consultations.

“There’s a distinct separation between these two things.”

Mr Usamate said Government needed to be careful not to assume that consultations conducted by the Executive meant Parliament had completed its own scrutiny.

He said adequate time was necessary to identify potential problems and ensure Fiji had a strong electoral system.

item.title: Call for stronger cooperation
item.description: THE Fiji Financial Intelligence Unit (FFIU) has come under scrutiny over the quality and effectiveness of intelligence reports it provides to law enforcement agencies, with Parliament told poor coordination is hampering investigations into financial crimes. Standing Committee on Economic Affairs chairman Sakiusa Tubuna presented the committee’s review of the FFIU 2024 Annual Report to Parliament o
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Financial Intelligence Unit (FFIU) has come under scrutiny over the quality and effectiveness of intelligence reports it provides to law enforcement agencies, with Parliament told poor coordination is hampering investigations into financial crimes.

Standing Committee on Economic Affairs chairman Sakiusa Tubuna presented the committee’s review of the FFIU 2024 Annual Report to Parliament on Wednesday.

The committee found that while the FFIU produced 237 intelligence products in 2024, there was no systematic feedback showing how many resulted in investigations, prosecutions, convictions or asset recoveries.

“The Fiji Police Force informed the committee that due to poor quality of intelligence reports, they have to spend more time and resources in conducting investigations,” Mr Tubuna said.

He said the committee also identified a lack of coordination between the FFIU, Fiji Police Force, FICAC and FRCS, warning this could prevent matters from being pursued through to prosecution.

Despite having only nine permanent and two seconded officers, the FFIU managed more than $37 million transaction reports, processed over $6.1million financial transactions and analysed 304 suspicious transaction reports.

Mr Tubuna said scams accounted for 38 per cent of disseminated intelligence cases in 2024, while tax-related offences represented about 86 per cent of the total transaction value linked to disseminated cases.

The committee called for stronger performance measurement, annual targets and clear benchmarks to allow Parliament and the public to assess the FFIU’s effectiveness and value for money.

It also urged stronger cooperation among agencies as Fiji faced growing threats from scams, tax crimes, money laundering, organised crime and corruption.

item.title: Fisheries tightening net on illegal fishing
item.description: FIJI has stepped up its fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, deploying satellite surveillance, mandatory vessel tracking, 100 per cent port inspections and naval patrols to protect its vast 1.2 million square kilometre exclusive economic zone. Minister for Fisheries and Forestry Alitia Bainivalu told Parliament on Wednesday that Fiji’s tuna fisheries were vital not only
item.content:encoded:
FIJI has stepped up its fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, deploying satellite surveillance, mandatory vessel tracking, 100 per cent port inspections and naval patrols to protect its vast 1.2 million square kilometre exclusive economic zone.

Minister for Fisheries and Forestry Alitia Bainivalu told Parliament on Wednesday that Fiji’s tuna fisheries were vital not only to the economy but also to the country’s food security and national identity.

“Our tuna fisheries are not merely an economic sector, they are an integral component of Fiji’s cultural heritage, national identity and food security,” she said.

Ms Bainivalu said IUU fishing threatened Fiji’s conservation efforts and sovereign wealth.

“If left unchecked, IUU fishing undermines decades of conservation work, sabotages the domestic economy, and steals the sovereign wealth of the Fijian people.”

She said Fiji had operationalised its Fisheries Surveillance and Operations Centre with the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency and was using real-time satellite imagery and vessel monitoring systems.

All foreign fishing vessels making port calls in Fiji are subjected to physical inspections, while risk assessments are conducted before vessels are granted entry.

Ms Bainivalu said Fiji was also extending enforcement into international waters through regional operations and Shiprider agreements.

Opposition MP Semi Koroilavesau welcomed the measures but warned that illegal fishing could also occur within Fiji’s licensed fleet.

“I also wish to add that illegal and unreported fishing also is within our own licensed fisheries,” he said.
